purpose: Structured, interconnected dog training and behaviour knowledge library for a reward-based, welfare-centred mobile app.
copyright_note: Sidekick's lesson library is an original synthesis, developed and checked against published welfare and training guidance from Dogs Trust, RSPCA, Blue Cross, Battersea, ABTC and AVSAB — see the evidence base below for the full breakdown.
progression_note: The 80/60/40 success rule is an app design heuristic, not a universal scientific threshold.

lessons.title: Choosing what to reward with
lessons.objective: Pick the reward(s) you'll use to start training, before the first session.
lessons.why_it_matters: Starting with a reward the dog will reliably work for makes every following lesson easier — this single choice affects how well the whole first week of training goes.
lessons.equipment: Small soft treats | A favourite toy
lessons.setup: Have a few candidate rewards ready to test.
lessons.steps: Offer 2-3 small, soft treats and note enthusiasm. | Note interest in a toy if food isn't strongly motivating. | Choose whichever produces the most reliable, eager response for these first sessions.
lessons.success_criteria: A reward is chosen that the dog reliably and eagerly works for in a quiet room.
lessons.common_mistakes: Increasing difficulty too quickly. | Repeating the cue instead of changing the setup. | Rewarding too late. | Training for too long.
lessons.regression: Reduce distance, duration or distraction. | Increase reward value. | Return to a familiar environment. | Shorten the session.
lessons.progression: Change only one difficulty dimension at a time. | Add mild distraction or duration. | Practise in another safe environment. | Gradually introduce competing rewards.
lessons.real_world_application: Practise the same skill in everyday contexts once the dog is succeeding in structured sessions.
lessons.professional_help_if: Behaviour is worsening, the dog appears distressed, or progress repeatedly stalls despite appropriate regression and management.
lessons.review_status: Initial release — review against current evidence before major app release

lessons.title: Practising marker timing
lessons.objective: Practise marking the exact instant a simple, naturally-occurring behaviour happens, to sharpen timing before it matters for a taught skill.
lessons.why_it_matters: Builds a useful behaviour while supporting clear communication, welfare and reliable real-world performance.
lessons.setup: Sit with the dog nearby with nothing specific being asked of them.
lessons.steps: Wait for any small, clear moment — a glance, a sit, a paw shift. | Mark the instant it happens, not a moment after. | Reward. | Repeat, paying close attention to how quickly the mark follows the behaviour.
lessons.success_criteria: Marker consistently lands within about half a second of the behaviour occurring.
lessons.common_mistakes: Marking slightly after the behaviour has already ended, which risks marking the wrong moment.

lessons.title: Understanding the prompt hierarchy

lessons.setup: No hands-on exercise — this is a planning step before fading prompts.

lessons.title: Adding a verbal cue to a known behaviour
lessons.objective: Attach a verbal cue to a behaviour only once it's already reliable with a prompt, so the word is linked to a real, existing behaviour rather than nothing.
lessons.why_it_matters: Builds a useful behaviour while supporting clear communication, welfare and reliable real-world performance.
lessons.setup: A behaviour the dog performs reliably with a prompt.
lessons.steps: Say the new verbal cue just before giving the usual prompt. | Perform the behaviour as normal. | Mark and reward. | Repeat consistently, always saying the cue in the same spot in the sequence, just before the prompt.
lessons.success_criteria: Cue and prompt are consistently paired across many repetitions before attempting the cue alone.
lessons.common_mistakes: Increasing difficulty too quickly. | Repeating the cue instead of changing the setup. | Rewarding too late. | Training for too long.
lessons.regression: Reduce distance, duration or distraction. | Increase reward value. | Return to a familiar environment. | Shorten the session.
lessons.progression: Change only one difficulty dimension at a time. | Add mild distraction or duration. | Practise in another safe environment. | Gradually introduce competing rewards.
lessons.real_world_application: Adding the cue too early, before the behaviour is reliable, is one of the most common reasons a cue never really 'sticks'.

lessons.title: Practising saying a cue only once
lessons.objective: Build the habit of giving a cue a single time and waiting, rather than repeating it when the dog doesn't respond immediately.
lessons.why_it_matters: Repeating a cue several times teaches the dog that the first (or second, or third) repetition doesn't actually matter — the opposite of what a reliable cue needs.
lessons.setup: A behaviour the dog knows reasonably well.
lessons.steps: Give the cue once, clearly. | Wait several seconds without repeating it. | If the dog responds, reward warmly. | If they don't, don't repeat the cue — instead, make the situation easier (closer, calmer, more obvious prompt) and try again.
lessons.success_criteria: Handler consistently gives a cue only once per attempt, adjusting difficulty rather than repeating the word.
lessons.common_mistakes: Repeating the cue multiple times in escalating tones when the dog doesn't respond immediately.
lessons.regression: Reduce distance, duration or distraction. | Increase reward value. | Return to a familiar environment. | Shorten the session.
lessons.progression: Change only one difficulty dimension at a time. | Add mild distraction or duration. | Practise in another safe environment. | Gradually introduce competing rewards.

lessons.why_it_matters: Dogs Trust and Blue Cross both highlight adjusting food portions when using food extensively for training — training treats have calories too, and should come from the dog's overall food intake, not simply be added on top indefinitely.
lessons.setup: Estimate roughly how many treats are used in a typical training day.
lessons.steps: Note the approximate amount of food used in training on a typical day. | Reduce the regular meal portion slightly to account for it, particularly for high-frequency training periods. | Consider using part of the dog's normal kibble ration as one of the reward types during training.
lessons.success_criteria: Overall food intake, including training rewards, stays appropriate for the dog's weight and needs.

lessons.title: Name response
lessons.objective: Teach the dog to immediately check in with the handler the instant they hear their name.
lessons.why_it_matters: Dogs Trust specifically advises against repeating the name multiple times when the dog isn't responding, since this can weaken the response over time — one clear cue, said once, matters more than volume or repetition.
lessons.setup: Wait for a moment when the dog is looking elsewhere, in a quiet environment.
lessons.steps: Wait until the dog's attention is elsewhere. | Say their name once, in a normal, upbeat tone. | The instant they look towards you, mark. | Reward. | Repeat across several sessions.
lessons.success_criteria: Dog responds to their name within 8 of 10 attempts.
lessons.common_mistakes: Repeating the name several times in a row when the dog doesn't respond immediately. | Saying the name in an angry tone. | Using the name right before something the dog finds unpleasant.
lessons.regression: Practise in an even quieter environment with a higher-value reward.
lessons.progression: Quiet room, 8/10 success → mild distraction → moderate distraction → reliable outdoors.
lessons.real_world_application: Practise the same skill in everyday contexts once the dog is succeeding in structured sessions.

lessons.title: Voluntary check-in
lessons.objective: Teach the dog that voluntarily looking towards the handler, with no cue given, is worthwhile.
lessons.why_it_matters: Dogs Trust specifically recommends rewarding spontaneous check-ins because they help build focus on the handler — this is the bridge between a dog that knows some tricks and a dog that actually pays attention.
lessons.setup: A quiet room with no particular distractions.
lessons.steps: Stand or sit quietly without calling the dog's name. | Allow them to investigate their surroundings freely. | The instant they glance towards you, mark. | Reward immediately. | Repeat, saying nothing and asking for nothing in between.
lessons.success_criteria: Dog voluntarily glances toward the handler with increasing frequency, unprompted.
lessons.common_mistakes: Calling the dog's name or otherwise prompting the look, which defeats the purpose of rewarding a voluntary check-in.
lessons.regression: Reduce distance, duration or distraction. | Increase reward value. | Return to a familiar environment. | Shorten the session.

lessons.title: Reward placement shapes behaviour
lessons.objective: Deliver rewards in a location that reinforces the intended behaviour, not just as payment after the fact.
lessons.why_it_matters: Where a reward is delivered matters — for recall, delivering the reward as the dog reaches the handler reinforces coming close. For a stay, delivering the reward while the dog remains in position reinforces staying put. For loose-lead walking, rewarding near the handler encourages staying close. The reward isn't just payment; it can actively help create the behaviour.
lessons.setup: Consider what position or location you want to reinforce before delivering any reward.

lessons.title: Rewarding loose lead early
lessons.objective: Reward the lead being slack the moment it happens, rather than waiting until the dog has already pulled.
lessons.why_it_matters: Battersea's guidance emphasises rewarding loose-lead walking and increasing difficulty gradually, rather than expecting perfect walking in a stimulating environment straight away. lessons.setup: Any walking environment, starting somewhere low-distraction.
lessons.steps: Watch the lead, not the dog's behaviour in general. | The instant it's slack, mark and reward. | Reward at that same slack point again and again before moving to a harder environment. | Avoid waiting for a 'good stretch' of walking — reward the moment the lead is loose, early and often at first.

lessons.title: Stop when the lead tightens
lessons.objective: Teach that a tight lead makes the walk stop, rather than the dog getting where it wants to go faster by pulling.
lessons.why_it_matters: If pulling reliably gets the dog closer to what it wants, pulling will continue. Removing that payoff — the walk simply pauses — is what makes the alternative worth learning.
lessons.setup: Any walk, ideally starting somewhere with only mild pulling triggers.
lessons.steps: As soon as the lead goes tight, stop moving completely. | Wait, without speaking or pulling back. | The moment the lead slackens (dog turns back, sits, or eases off), mark and reward. | Continue walking. | Repeat every time tension reappears.
lessons.success_criteria: Dog begins to ease off the lead voluntarily as tension builds, without needing repeated full stops.

lessons.regression: Practise in a lower-distraction area first, where tension happens less often and less intensely.

lessons.title: Recovering from a failed recall
lessons.objective: Respond constructively when a recall doesn't work, rather than repeating the cue louder or punishing the eventual return.
lessons.why_it_matters: Every repeated or ignored cue adds to a history of the cue not working. How the handler responds in the moment shapes whether recall gets stronger or weaker over time.
lessons.setup: No special setup — this is about what to do in the moment when recall fails.
lessons.steps: If the dog doesn't respond, don't repeat the cue loudly or chase. | Move away or make yourself interesting instead (crouch down, jog a few steps away) to invite the dog back voluntarily. | Once the dog returns, reward calmly — never punish a late return. | Afterwards, reduce difficulty for the next few repetitions rather than testing the same level again immediately.
lessons.success_criteria: Handler responds to a failed recall by reducing difficulty and rewarding the eventual return, rather than escalating pressure.
lessons.common_mistakes: Punishing the dog after they do eventually come back, which teaches them that returning is risky. | Repeating the cue many times, which devalues it further.
lessons.regression: Drop back to an easier, more reliable distance/environment for the next several sessions.
lessons.progression: Failed recall recognised early → difficulty reduced appropriately → recall rebuilt gradually back to the previous level.
lessons.real_world_application: Practise the same skill in everyday contexts once the dog is succeeding in structured sessions.

lessons.why_it_matters: Children move unpredictably, make unusual noises, and may run, grab, hug, or fall — none of which is necessarily how the dog has learned to read calm human behaviour. This deserves its own conservative progression rather than assuming general people-socialisation covers it.

lessons.steps: Start with children at a distance the dog can easily ignore or calmly observe. | Reward calm attention or disengagement. | Gradually reduce distance only as the dog stays relaxed. | Add movement and noise gradually rather than all at once. | Never allow unsupervised interaction, regardless of how comfortable the dog seems.

lessons.common_mistakes: Assuming a dog's comfort with calm adults transfers automatically to unpredictable child behaviour. | Allowing interaction before the dog has shown sustained comfort at distance.

lessons.title: Ending an interaction early
lessons.objective: Interrupt a dog-dog interaction calmly, before it escalates, using a practiced cue rather than physically pulling the dogs apart.
lessons.why_it_matters: Watching for early signs — avoidance, freezing, repeated attempts to escape, stiff posture, one dog persistently pursuing the other — means an interaction can be ended calmly, well before it needs a more dramatic intervention.

lessons.steps: Teach a neutral interrupt cue (e.g. 'this way') with no distraction present first. | Reward moving away with the handler on cue. | Introduce it during calm moments of dog-dog interaction, well before any tension. | Reward generously for disengaging. | Use it proactively at the first sign of discomfort in either dog, not as a last resort.

lessons.title: Handling foundations and reading discomfort
lessons.objective: Build a positive association with gentle touch, while learning to recognise the early signs that a dog is uncomfortable with handling.
lessons.why_it_matters: Many behaviours owners label as 'bad' during grooming or vet visits — turning away, freezing, growling — are actually the dog communicating discomfort. Dogs Trust specifically encourages owners to recognise these subtle signs and give the dog space rather than push through.
lessons.setup: Start in a calm, familiar environment with the dog relaxed and not restrained.
lessons.steps: Touch the shoulder briefly, mark, and reward. | Repeat on the chest, then the side, then the back. | Keep each session very short — a handful of touches is enough. | Watch for early discomfort signals throughout: turning away, lip licking, yawning, freezing, whale eye, moving away, stiffening. | If any of these appear, stop and reduce intensity rather than continuing.
lessons.success_criteria: Dog stays loose and relaxed through gentle touch on all four areas, with no discomfort signals present.
lessons.common_mistakes: Continuing to handle a dog that is showing subtle stress signals because they haven't growled or snapped yet.
lessons.regression: Shorten touches. | Return to an area the dog is already comfortable with before progressing.
lessons.progression: Touch → brief hold → gentle pressure → movement while touching → handling equipment introduced → examination-style handling.
lessons.real_world_application: Practise the same skill in everyday contexts once the dog is succeeding in structured sessions.

lessons.title: Doorbell desensitisation

lessons.why_it_matters: If the doorbell always means high-arousal visitors arriving, the sound itself becomes an alarm. The goal is for the doorbell to become something predictable and positive rather than an instruction to react.

lessons.title: Visitor arrival routine
lessons.objective: Break a visitor's arrival into separate stages so each part can be trained calmly, rather than treating it as one overwhelming event.
lessons.why_it_matters: A visitor arriving is actually several distinct events stacked together — the bell, movement to the door, the door opening, a person entering, that person moving around, interacting, and eventually leaving. Practising each stage separately makes the whole sequence far more manageable than trying to fix 'visitors' as one thing.
lessons.setup: Recruit a helper willing to repeat an arrival several times during training.
lessons.steps: Practise Stage 1 alone: doorbell sound, dog stays settled, reward. | Stage 2: handler walks to the door, dog stays settled, reward. | Stage 3: door opens, no one there yet, dog stays settled, reward. | Stage 4: helper enters, dog stays settled, reward. | Stage 5: helper moves around the room, dog stays settled, reward. | Stage 6: helper interacts briefly with the dog if calm, reward. | Stage 7: helper leaves, dog stays settled, reward. | Only combine stages once each works reliably alone.
lessons.success_criteria: Dog remains under threshold (no jumping, sustained barking, or bolting) through at least the first 4 stages combined.
lessons.common_mistakes: Increasing difficulty too quickly. | Repeating the cue instead of changing the setup. | Rewarding too late. | Training for too long.
lessons.regression: Go back to practising stages individually rather than combined. | Use a calmer, more familiar helper. | Increase the dog's distance from the door.
lessons.progression: Individual stages → two stages combined → full arrival sequence with a familiar helper → full sequence with a stranger.

lessons.title: Step away and return
lessons.objective: Build comfort with the handler stepping away and returning, starting from a single step and increasing very gradually.
lessons.why_it_matters: RSPCA guidance recommends increasing alone time gradually and returning to an easier stage if the dog reacts — the whole programme depends on never outpacing what the dog can currently cope with.
lessons.setup: Dog settled and comfortable on their bed, no signs of anxiety about the handler's presence.
lessons.steps: With the dog settled, take one step away. | Return immediately and reward calm behaviour. | Repeat, then extend to two steps, then five. | Progress to the doorway, then briefly outside the doorway. | Extend duration in seconds, then minutes, always returning before the dog shows distress.
lessons.success_criteria: Dog remains settled through each step of the progression, showing no anxious behaviour on the handler's return.
lessons.common_mistakes: Assuming 'they'll eventually get used to it' and pushing through visible distress, rather than treating that distress as a sign the previous step was too difficult.
lessons.regression: Return to the last step where the dog was clearly comfortable, and stay there longer before progressing again.
lessons.progression: 1 step → 2 steps → 5 steps → doorway → outside doorway → seconds away → minutes away.
lessons.real_world_application: Practise the same skill in everyday contexts once the dog is succeeding in structured sessions.
lessons.professional_help_if: The dog shows signs of significant distress (panic, attempts to escape, self-injury, continuous vocalising) even at the earliest steps — this needs professional support rather than continued gradual exposure alone.

lessons.title: Neutralising departure cues
lessons.objective: Reduce the anticipatory stress caused by cues like keys, coats, or the door, by disconnecting them from an actual departure.
lessons.why_it_matters: Dogs can learn that picking up keys, putting on a coat, or opening the door reliably predicts being left — which means anxiety can start building well before the owner has even left. Making these cues 'boring' by repeating them without leaving reduces that anticipation.
lessons.equipment: Keys | Coat | Bag — whatever the dog's specific departure cues are
lessons.setup: Practise at a calm time, not right before an actual departure.
lessons.steps: Pick up the keys, then sit back down without leaving. | Put the coat on, then take it off and continue as normal. | Open the door, then close it again. | Repeat each of these individually, in no particular order, several times a day. | Continue until the dog no longer reacts to these cues at all.
lessons.success_criteria: Dog shows no anticipatory anxiety (pacing, following, vocalising) when departure cues occur without an actual departure.
lessons.common_mistakes: Only ever performing these cues immediately before really leaving, which is exactly what keeps them predictive of departure.
lessons.regression: Practise the cues more frequently, in smaller isolated pieces, before combining them.
lessons.progression: Individual cues neutralised → cues combined → cues followed by brief actual departures.

lessons.title: Diagnosing why the dog is barking
lessons.objective: Identify which of several possible categories is driving the barking, since the right response depends entirely on the cause.
lessons.why_it_matters: A single 'stop barking' approach doesn't work because barking can come from very different places — alerting, fear, frustration, excitement, seeking attention, play, territorial behaviour, separation distress, boredom, pain, or simply a learned habit. Each of these calls for a different response.
lessons.setup: Observe the barking across several occurrences rather than diagnosing from a single incident.
lessons.steps: Note what happens immediately before the barking starts. | Consider which category best fits: alerting, fear, frustration, excitement, attention-seeking, play, territorial, separation distress, boredom, pain/discomfort, or learned behaviour. | Note what happens immediately after the barking — what does it achieve for the dog? | Use this to choose the matching approach from the other barking lessons, rather than a generic 'quiet' cue alone.
lessons.success_criteria: Owner can identify the most likely category driving their dog's barking in a specific context.
lessons.common_mistakes: Assuming all barking has the same cause and applying the same fix regardless of context.
lessons.regression: Reduce distance, duration or distraction. | Increase reward value. | Return to a familiar environment. | Shorten the session.
lessons.progression: Change only one difficulty dimension at a time. | Add mild distraction or duration. | Practise in another safe environment. | Gradually introduce competing rewards.

lessons.title: Building towards a 'quiet' cue
lessons.objective: Build a genuine 'quiet' cue by rewarding the pause in barking first, only adding the word once the dog understands what's being rewarded.
lessons.why_it_matters: A cue only means something once it's reliably paired with the behaviour it's meant to produce. Adding the word 'quiet' before the dog has a strong history of being rewarded for pausing just adds noise without teaching anything yet.
lessons.setup: Wait for a natural bout of barking to work with, rather than provoking one.
lessons.steps: Allow the dog to bark naturally. | Wait for any pause, even brief. | The instant they're quiet, mark and reward. | Repeat across several barking episodes, rewarding the pause each time. | Once pausing reliably follows a consistent brief delay, add the word 'quiet' just before the pause typically happens. | Continue rewarding the quiet moment after the cue.
lessons.success_criteria: Dog reliably pauses barking within a few seconds of the 'quiet' cue.
lessons.common_mistakes: Introducing the word before the dog has a reward history for pausing, so the cue doesn't yet mean anything.
lessons.regression: Return to rewarding any pause without the cue word, rebuilding the pattern before reintroducing it.
lessons.progression: Reward any pause → reward a slightly longer pause → cue added → cue reliably followed by quiet.

lessons.title: Understanding the chase cycle

lessons.why_it_matters: Chasing follows a natural sequence — see, orient, stalk, chase, catch — and every successful chase can reinforce the behaviour for next time. This makes management just as much a part of training as any specific exercise.
lessons.equipment: None — this is an observation and planning step
lessons.setup: Observe the dog's typical triggers (squirrels, rabbits, birds, cats, cyclists, runners, cars) to know what to watch for.
lessons.steps: Notice the earliest stage: the dog seeing a potential target. | Notice orienting — body and attention turning towards it. | If stalking begins, this is the last easy point to intervene before a chase starts. | Once a chase begins, it's much harder to interrupt — prevention at the earlier stages matters far more than a cue used too late. | Use distance and management to prevent rehearsal of the full cycle wherever possible.

lessons.progression: Change only one difficulty dimension at a time. | Add mild distraction or duration. | Practise in another safe environment. | Gradually introduce competing rewards.

lessons.title: Finding the working threshold distance
lessons.objective: Find the distance at which the dog can notice a trigger and stay calm — the distance training actually happens at, not the distance you eventually want to reach.
lessons.why_it_matters: Distance isn't failure — it's training equipment. The training zone is the distance where the dog is currently comfortable, which is often much further away than owners expect, not the close distance that represents the eventual goal.

lessons.setup: Use a known trigger and a large, open space where distance can be controlled.
lessons.steps: Start at a distance where the dog notices the trigger but shows no tension — calm. | Note this distance. | Move slightly closer and note when the dog becomes interested but not yet worried. | Continue closer and note when tension appears (early body-language signals). | Note the distance at which a full reaction occurs. | Use the calm-to-tense range as your current working zone — not the reactive distance.
lessons.success_criteria: A rough threshold map exists: calm distance, interested distance, tense distance, reactive distance.
lessons.common_mistakes: Training at the distance you want to eventually reach, rather than the distance that's currently manageable.
lessons.regression: If the dog reacts at the assumed 'calm' distance, the true threshold is further away than recorded — increase distance and reassess.

lessons.title: Counter-conditioning at a safe distance
lessons.objective: Change how the dog feels about a trigger by consistently pairing its appearance with something wonderful, at a distance where the dog can stay calm throughout.
lessons.why_it_matters: This is not the same as flooding. Deliberately exposing a frightened or reactive dog to a trigger at overwhelming intensity risks making things worse, not better — the whole method depends on staying at a distance the dog can cope with. Repeated exposure doesn't automatically help, either — done carelessly it can make a response stronger rather than weaker (sensitisation), which is exactly why distance and pacing matter so much here.
lessons.equipment: Very high-value treats reserved for this exercise
lessons.setup: Identify the dog's working threshold distance first (see the threshold lesson) before starting.
lessons.steps: Trigger appears at the working distance. | Immediately deliver a high-value reward, repeatedly, for as long as the trigger is visible. | Reward stops the moment the trigger is out of sight. | Repeat across many short sessions rather than one long one. | Only decrease distance once the dog shows a consistently relaxed, positive response at the current distance.
lessons.success_criteria: Dog's body language shifts to anticipating the reward when the trigger appears, rather than showing tension.
lessons.common_mistakes: Working too close, too soon, which risks the opposite emotional pairing forming. | Treating this as a one-off exercise rather than many repeated, short sessions.
lessons.regression: Increase distance further. | Shorten sessions.
lessons.progression: Trigger at a large, easy distance → gradually reduced distance → trigger passing at a normal working distance.
lessons.real_world_application: Practise the same skill in everyday contexts once the dog is succeeding in structured sessions.
lessons.professional_help_if: The dog cannot calm down even at a large distance, or shows a severe fear response — this needs professional guidance before continuing.

lessons.why_it_matters: A dog that had a poor night's sleep, an unexpected visitor, a noisy delivery, and a busy walk may react more intensely to a normally-manageable trigger later that day. Recording these events prevents owners from reading every reaction as evidence that training isn't working.
lessons.setup: Keep a simple log of stressful events across the day, not just training sessions.
lessons.steps: Note any potentially stressful event through the day — poor sleep, a visitor, a loud noise, an earlier dog encounter, a busy walk. | If a reaction happens later that day, check the log for stacking before assuming training has regressed. | On days with several logged stressors, consider a lower-key training session or a rest day instead.
lessons.success_criteria: Owner can identify likely trigger-stacking days in hindsight and adjusts expectations or plans accordingly.
lessons.common_mistakes: Increasing difficulty too quickly. | Repeating the cue instead of changing the setup. | Rewarding too late. | Training for too long.
lessons.regression: Reduce distance, duration or distraction. | Increase reward value. | Return to a familiar environment. | Shorten the session.
lessons.progression: Change only one difficulty dimension at a time. | Add mild distraction or duration. | Practise in another safe environment. | Gradually introduce competing rewards.
lessons.real_world_application: This is often what separates 'my training isn't working' from 'today was a genuinely hard day for my dog' — the same dog, the same skills, but a different starting point.

lessons.title: Shaping: letting the dog figure it out
lessons.objective: Teach a new behaviour by rewarding successive small steps toward it, rather than luring or telling the dog exactly what to do.
lessons.why_it_matters: Shaping develops problem-solving and offers a genuine mental workout — the dog is doing the thinking, not just following a lure.
lessons.equipment: A target object (box, platform) | Treats | A marker (clicker or verbal)
lessons.setup: Choose a simple target object to start, like a box or a low platform.
lessons.steps: Reward the dog for simply approaching the object. | Once that's reliable, only reward when they touch it. | Then only reward a paw touch. | Then two paws. | Continue shaping toward the final behaviour in small increments, only rewarding slightly more each time.
lessons.success_criteria: Dog offers increasingly specific behaviours toward the object without being lured or physically guided.
lessons.common_mistakes: Raising the criteria too quickly, which can cause the dog to stop offering behaviours altogether out of frustration.
lessons.regression: Return to rewarding the previous, easier step for a few more reps before raising criteria again.
lessons.progression: Change only one difficulty dimension at a time. | Add mild distraction or duration. | Practise in another safe environment. | Gradually introduce competing rewards.
lessons.real_world_application: Shaping is a genuinely different mental workout from cued behaviours, and many dogs find the problem-solving itself rewarding.

lessons.title: Thinking functionally about behaviour
lessons.objective: Ask what a behaviour is achieving for the dog, rather than assuming it's naughtiness or defiance.
lessons.why_it_matters: Dogs aren't generally trying to be naughty, dominant, spiteful, or deliberately disobedient — behaviours persist because they've worked before, or reflect emotional state, genetics, environment, learning history, or physical condition. lessons.equipment: None — this is a thinking framework, not a hands-on exercise

lessons.title: Matching reward value to difficulty
lessons.objective: Recognise that a reward's value isn't fixed — it changes with context — and increase reward value as a situation gets harder.
lessons.why_it_matters: Kibble in a quiet kitchen might be a strong reward, but the same kibble next to another dog may barely register, while chicken in that same distracting context might still work well. lessons.success_criteria: Reward value scales with difficulty, rather than the same reward being used regardless of context.

lessons.title: Building a separate emergency recall
lessons.objective: Build one cue, kept completely separate from everyday recall, reserved for genuine emergencies and backed by the highest-value reward the dog knows.
lessons.why_it_matters: An emergency cue that's only ever used for true emergencies, and always pays out enormously, stays reliable precisely because it's never been allowed to fail or feel routine.

lessons.setup: Choose a cue never used for anything else — a distinct word or sound.
lessons.steps: Choose a unique cue completely separate from the everyday recall word. | Pair it with the jackpot reward in a calm, low-distraction setting. | Practise only occasionally, always with the same huge reward. | Do not use it in ordinary situations, so it never has the chance to fail or feel unremarkable. | Test sparingly in controlled, safe setups as reliability builds.
lessons.success_criteria: Dog responds instantly and reliably to the emergency cue in the rare controlled tests it's given.
lessons.common_mistakes: Using the emergency cue for routine recalls, which erodes exactly what makes it different.
lessons.regression: Return to a calmer, lower-distraction environment and rebuild the jackpot association before testing again.
lessons.progression: Jackpot pairing at home → occasional controlled tests → reserved exclusively for real emergencies.

lessons.title: Responding to fear signals before they escalate
lessons.objective: Recognise fear-specific body language early, and respond by reducing intensity rather than pushing through exposure.
lessons.why_it_matters: Dogs Trust refers to subtle signals like yawning, leaning away, and changes around the eyes as useful 'whispers' that indicate discomfort — the goal is to respond when you see the whisper, not wait for the shout. Fear indicators specifically (crouching, retreating, a tucked tail, trembling, refusing food, attempting to escape) call for a different response than simple mild discomfort: don't force continued exposure.
lessons.setup: This is a recognition-and-response framework, not a hands-on training exercise.
lessons.steps: Watch for fear indicators: crouching, retreating, a tucked or low tail, avoidance, freezing, trembling, attempts to escape, hiding, or refusing food. | If these appear, don't continue with whatever triggered them. | Reduce intensity immediately — more distance, quieter environment, less pressure. | Create a sense of safety before attempting anything further. | Once calm, pair the trigger with positive experiences at a much easier level, and progress far more gradually than originally planned.
lessons.success_criteria: Owner recognises fear-specific signals and responds by reducing intensity and creating safety, rather than continuing the original plan.
lessons.common_mistakes: Continuing an exercise because the dog 'just needs to get used to it', when fear signals suggest the opposite response is needed.
lessons.regression: Reduce distance, duration or distraction. | Increase reward value. | Return to a familiar environment. | Shorten the session.
lessons.progression: Change only one difficulty dimension at a time. | Add mild distraction or duration. | Practise in another safe environment. | Gradually introduce competing rewards.
lessons.real_world_application: Give the dog distance, choice, time, and a quieter environment whenever fear signals appear — across any context in the library, not just formal reactivity work.

lessons.why_it_matters: Builds a useful behaviour while supporting clear communication, welfare and reliable real-world performance.
lessons.setup: Compare this context to where the behaviour is reliable — what's actually different?
lessons.steps: Identify what's different about this specific location or situation. | Change only that one variable back to an easier level. | Rebuild success at that easier level before reintroducing the harder version. | Avoid assuming the dog has forgotten the behaviour altogether.
lessons.success_criteria: The behaviour returns once the specific harder variable is addressed individually.
lessons.common_mistakes: Increasing difficulty too quickly. | Repeating the cue instead of changing the setup. | Rewarding too late. | Training for too long.
lessons.regression: Reduce distance, duration or distraction. | Increase reward value. | Return to a familiar environment. | Shorten the session.
lessons.progression: Change only one difficulty dimension at a time. | Add mild distraction or duration. | Practise in another safe environment. | Gradually introduce competing rewards.

lessons.title: My dog seems to be regressing
lessons.objective: Check for likely causes of a sudden decline before assuming lost progress.
lessons.why_it_matters: A sudden regression often has a specific, identifiable cause — illness, trigger stacking, a change in routine — rather than reflecting the dog 'forgetting' something previously reliable. A previously-reduced behaviour can also normally reappear briefly after a break in practice — this 'spontaneous recovery' doesn't mean training has failed, just that learning isn't always a perfectly straight line.
lessons.setup: Consider recent changes in health, routine, or environment.
lessons.steps: Rule out illness or pain first, especially if the change was sudden. | Consider recent stressful events that might have accumulated (trigger stacking). | Consider any change in routine, environment, or household. | If no clear cause is found, simply rebuild at an easier level for a few sessions rather than assuming a deeper problem. | Consider developmental stage too — adolescence commonly brings a temporary dip in focus and impulse control, and senior dogs can show new confusion, altered sleep, or reduced responsiveness worth a vet check.
lessons.success_criteria: A plausible cause is identified, or the behaviour recovers quickly once briefly rebuilt at an easier level.
lessons.common_mistakes: Increasing difficulty too quickly. | Repeating the cue instead of changing the setup. | Rewarding too late. | Training for too long.

lessons.progression: Change only one difficulty dimension at a time. | Add mild distraction or duration. | Practise in another safe environment. | Gradually introduce competing rewards.
lessons.real_world_application: Practise the same skill in everyday contexts once the dog is succeeding in structured sessions.

lessons.title: I keep repeating my cues
lessons.objective: Break the habit of repeating a cue multiple times, which weakens its meaning over time.

lessons.setup: Notice how many times a cue is typically said before a response.
lessons.steps: Say the cue once. | Wait several seconds in silence. | If there's no response, don't repeat the word — instead make the situation easier and try again. | Practise this discipline even when it's tempting to just repeat the word.

lessons.success_criteria: Owner recognises an over-threshold state and prioritises exit and recovery over continued training, when it happens.

lessons.common_mistakes: Increasing difficulty too quickly. | Repeating the cue instead of changing the setup. | Rewarding too late. | Training for too long.
lessons.objective: Extend the café routine to a typically harder environment — more people, more noise, more food, more movement, and often other dogs.
lessons.why_it_matters: A pub setting stacks several difficulty dimensions at once compared to a quiet café, so it's a natural next step once the café routine is solid, not a starting point.
lessons.setup: Choose a quieter pub or a quieter time of day for the first attempts.
lessons.equipment: A mat or towel | Treats | A settle aid
lessons.steps: Apply the same café-dog routine — settle on a mat, ignore food and people, calm departure. | Expect a harder baseline given the noise and activity level, and adjust duration accordingly. | If another dog is present, manage distance rather than assuming an automatic greeting is appropriate. | Reward generously for maintaining settle despite the higher activity level.
lessons.success_criteria: Dog maintains a settled state for a reasonable portion of the visit, coping with more noise, people, and movement than the café setting.
lessons.regression: Return to café-level environments until settle is very solid there.
lessons.progression: Quiet pub, short visit → busier pub → full evening visit.

lessons.title: Car travel routine
lessons.evidence_level: 🟠 Practical/app-generated framework based on established principles
lessons.review_status: Initial release — review against current evidence before major app release
lessons.common_mistakes: Only ever practising the exit at exciting destinations, which reinforces jumping out impulsively.
lessons.objective: Build a calm car routine — approaching, entering, settling, travelling, and exiting safely — as its own trained sequence.
lessons.why_it_matters: Each part of a car journey can be trained separately, and exiting matters as much as the rest — a dog should never be allowed to jump out of a vehicle into an unsafe environment, regardless of how excited they are to arrive.
lessons.setup: A parked, stationary car for the earliest steps, with journeys only introduced once entry and settling are solid.
lessons.equipment: Suitable travel restraint (crate, harness, or barrier) | Treats
lessons.steps: Practise calm approach to the car without it going anywhere yet. | Reward entering and settling in the travel restraint. | Take very short, uneventful journeys around the block. | Gradually extend journey length. | On arrival, ask for a calm, controlled exit — never allow the dog to jump straight out into an unsafe environment such as a road.
lessons.success_criteria: Dog settles for the journey and exits under control on cue, rather than launching out of the vehicle.
lessons.regression: Return to very short, low-stakes journeys.
lessons.progression: Stationary car → short local journeys → longer journeys → controlled exit at exciting destinations.

lessons.title: Busy town
lessons.evidence_level: 🟠 Practical/app-generated framework based on established principles
lessons.review_status: Initial release — review against current evidence before major app release
lessons.common_mistakes: Increasing difficulty too quickly. | Repeating the cue instead of changing the setup. | Rewarding too late. | Training for too long.
lessons.objective: Combine focus, loose-lead walking, direction changes, leave, settle, and trigger management into a single busy real-world walk.
lessons.why_it_matters: A busy town environment draws on nearly everything in the library at once — this is one of the most demanding real-world settings and should only be attempted once each individual skill is solid separately.
lessons.setup: Choose a moderately busy time first, building towards genuinely busy periods.
lessons.equipment: Lead | Treats | Long line not typically needed here given the lead-only environment
lessons.steps: Maintain loose-lead walking as the baseline throughout. | Use a direction-change cue proactively around any trigger that appears. | Use leave for dropped food or interesting items on the ground. | Take brief settle breaks if the environment becomes overwhelming. | Manage distance from any specific triggers (other dogs, loud sounds) using skills built elsewhere in the library.
lessons.success_criteria: Dog maintains a loose lead and manageable arousal through a genuinely busy environment, with the handler able to apply any of the component skills as needed.
lessons.regression: Return to quieter environments and rebuild individual components there before combining them again.
lessons.progression: Moderately busy → genuinely busy → busy environment with an added specific trigger.

lessons.title: Holiday-ready checklist
lessons.evidence_level: 🟠 Practical/app-generated framework based on established principles
lessons.review_status: Initial release — review against current evidence before major app release
lessons.common_mistakes: Increasing difficulty too quickly. | Repeating the cue instead of changing the setup. | Rewarding too late. | Training for too long.
lessons.objective: Prepare for travelling with the dog by working through a checklist of situations and practical items, rather than assuming everything will be fine on the day.
lessons.why_it_matters: Many holiday-related problems come from a genuinely new combination of unfamiliar things happening all at once — reviewing this checklist in advance means most of it is already familiar by the time it matters.
lessons.setup: Work through this checklist gradually in the weeks before travelling, rather than all at once.
lessons.equipment: Travel documentation | Familiar bedding | Usual food | Any medication
lessons.steps: Practise or confirm comfort with car journeys. | Consider how the dog will cope with new accommodation. | Consider exposure to new people and new dogs likely to be encountered. | Practise on a few different walking locations and surfaces if possible beforehand. | Check recall reliability in unfamiliar, safe locations before relying on it away from home. | Prepare practical items: emergency contact details, identification, any medication, familiar food, familiar bedding, and basic emergency supplies.
lessons.real_world_application: Car journey | New accommodation | New people | New dogs | New walking locations | Different surfaces | Restaurant or café | Beach | Recall reliability | Emergency contact | Identification | Medication | Food | Familiar bedding | Emergency supplies
lessons.success_criteria: Most checklist items have already been practised or prepared before the trip, rather than being addressed for the first time while away.

lessons.title: Building frustration tolerance
lessons.evidence_level: 🟠 Practical/app-generated framework based on established principles
lessons.review_status: Initial release — review against current evidence before major app release
lessons.common_mistakes: Extending delays too quickly, which risks teaching frustration rather than tolerance.
lessons.objective: Teach the dog that 'not immediately' doesn't mean 'never', using small, gradually increasing moments of delay.
lessons.why_it_matters: The objective isn't obedience achieved through frustration — it's teaching the dog that they can cope with a short wait, which supports calmness across nearly every other area of training.
lessons.setup: Choose an everyday moment that already involves a brief pause, and make the pause itself the exercise.
lessons.equipment: A toy | A food-filled container | Treats
lessons.steps: Briefly hold a toy behind your back before giving it, extending the delay only in small increments. | Use a food-filled container that takes a few seconds to access. | Build in brief waits before a door opens, before a release, or before being given a toy. | Reward calm waiting, not just the eventual access. | Keep delays very short at first, extending gradually only as the dog copes well.
lessons.success_criteria: Dog waits calmly through small, increasing delays across a range of everyday situations, without escalating frustration.
lessons.regression: Shorten delays significantly and rebuild more gradually.
lessons.progression: Very brief delay → longer delay → delay across a range of different everyday contexts.
lessons.real_world_application: This underpins coping with everyday waits — at doors, before meals, before walks — without escalating into whining, barking, or jumping.

lessons.title: Understanding classical conditioning
lessons.evidence_level: 🟠 Practical/app-generated framework based on established principles
lessons.review_status: Initial release — review against current evidence before major app release
lessons.common_mistakes: Increasing difficulty too quickly. | Repeating the cue instead of changing the setup. | Rewarding too late. | Training for too long.
lessons.objective: Understand classical conditioning as a separate mechanism from teaching a behaviour — building an association between a neutral event and an emotional response.
lessons.why_it_matters: This principle underlies a huge amount of behaviour modification work — reactivity, fear, vet visits, grooming, harnesses, car journeys, visitors, noises, and separation all rely on changing an emotional association, not teaching a new behaviour.
lessons.setup: No hands-on exercise here — this concept explains why many other lessons in the library work the way they do.
lessons.steps: Understand the basic pattern: a neutral event (a cupboard opening) is repeatedly followed by something meaningful (food appearing). | Over time, the neutral event itself starts to produce the emotional response (excitement) on its own. | Recognise that this is the mechanism behind desensitisation and counter-conditioning work used throughout the reactivity, handling, and alone-time sections of the library.
lessons.success_criteria: Owner can explain, in their own words, why pairing a neutral trigger with something positive changes how a dog feels about that trigger.
lessons.real_world_application: Doorbell desensitisation, harness conditioning, and counter-conditioning around reactive triggers are all direct applications of this single principle.

lessons.title: Finding your dog's reward currency
lessons.evidence_level: 🟠 Practical/app-generated framework based on established principles
lessons.review_status: Initial release — review against current evidence before major app release
lessons.common_mistakes: Increasing difficulty too quickly. | Repeating the cue instead of changing the setup. | Rewarding too late. | Training for too long.
lessons.objective: Build a personalised sense of what this specific dog finds rewarding, and roughly how much, rather than assuming a standard list applies.
lessons.why_it_matters: Dogs Trust explicitly recommends thinking broadly about what individual dogs find rewarding — one dog's jackpot is another dog's non-event, and knowing the difference makes every other lesson easier to teach well.
lessons.setup: Observe the dog across a range of situations, not just during dedicated training.
lessons.steps: Note how enthusiastically the dog responds to different food rewards (kibble, cheese, chicken). | Note interest in toys, tugging, or fetching. | Note interest in praise alone, sniffing opportunities, and running. | Rate each roughly from low to very high value for this individual dog. | Revisit this periodically, since preferences can shift.
lessons.success_criteria: A rough personal reward hierarchy exists for this dog, covering food and non-food rewards.
lessons.real_world_application: This personalised hierarchy is what makes it possible to match reward value to difficulty, rather than guessing.

lessons.title: Using life rewards
lessons.evidence_level: 🟠 Practical/app-generated framework based on established principles
lessons.review_status: Initial release — review against current evidence before major app release
lessons.common_mistakes: Increasing difficulty too quickly. | Repeating the cue instead of changing the setup. | Rewarding too late. | Training for too long.
lessons.objective: Use access to something the dog already wants — sniffing, greeting, going outside — as a reward for a small piece of good behaviour first.
lessons.why_it_matters: This is a genuinely powerful concept: rather than treating the environment as competition for the dog's attention, it becomes part of the training system itself. A dog that walks nicely for a short stretch and then gets released to sniff learns that good behaviour is what unlocks the things they already wanted.
lessons.setup: Identify something the dog clearly wants in the moment — a sniff, a greeting, access to a room.
lessons.equipment: None beyond what's already in the environment
lessons.steps: Notice something the dog wants access to right now. | Ask for a small, achievable piece of good behaviour first (a few steps of loose lead, a brief sit). | Release them to the thing they wanted as the reward, using a consistent release word. | Apply this pattern across many everyday moments, not just formal training sessions.
lessons.success_criteria: The dog's own environment and everyday wants are being used as a functional part of training, not just food.
lessons.real_world_application: Loose-lead walking rewarded with 'go sniff', waiting at a door rewarded with being let outside, and a brief sit rewarded with being greeted are all examples of the same principle.
